title: Do you think the Australian film industry will become more successful?

commenti.body:
Well, usually major studios need to establish a system in other countries to develop projects there. If you are looking for an opportunity to work in the system you will need to be where the system is. You can work outside of it and then strive to receive recognition, primarily through film festivals and networking. If you can acquire an agent or manager to get you in the room then certainly that can and should help. Still, film festivals are still safe in some capacity, especially the major ones because now festivals are cash-grabs but screening films at a festival like Sundance, luckily can open few doors. That is precisely what the brothers who directed Talk to Me did, got distribution through screening their film at Sundance but it is a very difficult festival to get your film in. Now, Australia and even the United Kingdom have a volatile industry. It is not even an industry but people who carve out a niche and build their business around it and through it get recognized. The best bet is to make a feature film with resources you have. Try making the best, thoughtful, creative, meaning and engaging film you can. Find distribution or an agent/manager, accumulate significant amounts of feedback then have few more ideas in your hand so that you can show your versatility to execs and producers because obviously they will not let you remake what you made. They want to see if you can work under their guidelines and control, and do what you did but this time with some success either critically or with box office numbers. This usually what people who want to become directors will want to do if they want to make it in right now because the industry is saturated. Anyone can make a film from anywhere, receive acclaim and possibly get opportunities. There are many platforms and channels that allow people to have their work seen but if you are lucky you will make it. Otherwise, make your feature film, get it out there and receive praise through private screenings, festival screenings maybe (might sound absurd) use your YouTube feedback and do some sort of poll and ask your audience if they want something more out of you. Prove it to people who have resources to help you that you are capable of making a good film, handle the job properly and bring everything together with ease or gather people together, form your own production team of sorts with like-minded people. Make something bigger and better than your first film with that team, do gorilla marketing, organically generate praise through various screenings to corroborate to a distributor for distributing your film through a streaming service, limited theatrical release or you can even publish your feature film on Amazon Prime yourself. 

Australia is not yet lucrative enough to be considered as an industry. Most talented people reach out to Hollywood or do something else entirely even after say making a few films of their own and probably getting nowhere. 

If you want to be a cinematographer, audio engineer, editor etc. then build your portfolio. Find and build a network to afford the leverage of getting in the business. Keep growing, experimenting and try new things. Film schools and festivals. Only the prestigious ones can get you somewhere if you are completely lost but even there you need to go with an open-mind. All the people participating and enrolling in these places want to do what you want to do as well and it takes one with sheer determination, talent and perseverance to become a filmmaker who has passed the threshold now has to lay the foundation of their future because that is always uncertain. 

I hope this in some capacity answers your question. I apologize for any errors or if I am not to the point. Just thought I should share this if you are looking into doing something in the industry… 
Ask me anything else you’d like to, and I will try to help!

Where in Aus are you located OP? The reason I ask is that the biggest hurdle in Aus film right now IMO is how segmented the Industry is with every state having its own way of doing things.  I am in VIC and I get envious of my counterparts in NSW and QLD every time I hear about stories of how a new director gets funding from a production company based in QLD or NSW. Not to say film Victoria is bad but the opportunities seem to far lesser


If you go back to the history of Hollywood, Charlie Chaplin and a few others started United Artists and soon production companies all over the US came to Hollywood to centralise the film Industry. This is what I believe is lacking in Aus

Yes this is super super helpful and definitely puts me at ease lol. I will for sure take your advice. I know Sydney Film Festival (the state i live in) is somewhat of a big deal here, we have all sorts of stuff within the community. I agree I don’t think it counts as an “industry” just because of how small it is compared to other actual industries which is a shame. What do you think about studying? I found a university that apparently gets you making multiple films a year with all their facilities and equipment available. It sounds fantastic but not sure if it’s worth the fee. Most of all I worry about the networking. So much relies on networking in creative industries to the point where it’s impossible to guess if you’ll meet the right people in the next step or not. Not sure if that makes any sense but wonder what you think.
Perfectly said. This is the same problem in the UK as well.

I was initially aspiring to go to film school myself. My mains were NYU, USC, UCLA, SCAD, etc. You get the gist. But then you look at the alumni and how rare it is for anyone to break in. There are many perks of going to a film school but it has be the best of the best and that comes with unfathomable cost of admission and debt. The people there are talented and striving to find their place. Most end up doing nothing because there are no jobs are film school and that is the first mistake most students make. The idea of a film school is to learn, delve into the deeper nuances of the industry, how you should navigate in it and what should you do to be successful. You build your portfolio and work on set because to become a professional you need to know how professional equipment works and what it is like to be on a professional set. Film school is also designed for networking. Many students come together and form a production company of sorts or a super group to make their own feature film after they are done. They all have portfolios and all put each of themselves into the project, these are usually rare but a lot of people get together through such connections. Acquaintances you keep in touch with can help you someday in the long run. Basically the idea is to leverage your network, keep building new connections and you may land a job for someone, somewhere, somehow. 
Now, if you genuinely want to become a filmmaker and can learn most of this on your own, which you truly can with all the resources available online then you can invest that money on your own project. Teach yourself on how the equipment works. Hire students who graduated from film schools or hire professionals who would want to collaborate. If you have management and leadership skills then you can certainly make a film. After doing that send it to a film festival or try distributing it yourself or finding someone who can help you. I am sure people in Australia have connections and there are studios or production houses in Australia who can assist you because you have a complete product which you made on your own with what you have. A good underdog story. They can guide you and see sometimes you have to take a leap of faith.

Please someone make some modern westerns set in early settled Australia. That era is ripe for some incredible films.


I think Australia has the potential to make some incredible films. The issue is the scale I suppose. The setting of Australia lends itself to large scale, dramatic projects. Countries developing their film industries, are helped by smaller scale cheaper to make projects. Think Kitchen sink dramas in the UK, quirky comedy in NZ or darkly comedic character drama in Italy. The Oz film industry could do with a few artists to spur forward a version of this and it could well develop from there.

I wonder if there's too much of a focus on movies versus TV shows. Australia makes some great TV shows, and streamers looking for english content have helped with that. Even the stuff that the ABC puts out is surprisingly good given the relatively small market.
You should Audition for Mad Max, that’s set in Australia

The Australian New Wave did include some great films that made full use of the country's landscape: *Walkabout*, *Picnic at Hanging Rock*. 

I'd put the much more recent *Sweet Country* in that category -- it's like an Australian western, with all of that genre's sweep and its sublimity of tiny human figures in a great landscape. Warwick Thornton is definitely an Australian filmmaker to look out for. He usually works as his own cinematographer and at times creates almost Fordian images.

In my opinion you usually don't make a living doing films / short films. You make a living "doing commercials or mediocre cable TV shows". 

The films and short films are things you do in your spare time with the contacts, experience, and resources you've acquired during your "day job". At least that is how it works for 99% of creatives outside of Hollywood, and probably 97% of creatives *in* Hollywood.

Btw, have you ever dropped in at /r/AustralianFilm ?

What would success look like for the Australian film industry?

It doesn't have the population to sustain anything beyond a small independent industry. Domestic box office is enough to make major successes for Hollywood and Bollywood. 

And then it's cursed (or blessed) by sharing a language with America which means it will have an occasional break out success but all of its best and brightest will aspire to work in Hollywood, unlike European countries, with similar populations, where the language barrier, and desire for films in those languages, fosters longer careers in their home nation.
